The Six Chapters Spoken at the Site of Enlightenment, Eleven Fascicles. First Assembly: The Six Chapters Spoken at the Site of Enlightenment, Eleven Fascicles.

Chapter One: The Exquisite Array of the World Lords (*Lokendra-vyuha*). This sutra consists of thirty-nine chapters; only the "Immeasurable" (*Asaṃkhyeya*) chapter and the "Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiant Merits" chapter were spoken by the Buddha himself, while all others were added by various bodhisattvas. At the beginning, the Buddha was at the Bodhimaṇḍa in the forest retreat (*āraṇya-dharma*) of Magadha, having just attained perfect enlightenment.
It further states:
"By the Buddha's spiritual power, all the adornments of this site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) are made to appear therein.

This means that since [the Buddha's] lifespan is of a different duration than what was previously established, it differs from the traces left spontaneously beneath the Bodhi tree as described in the *Āgamas*; this is the teaching of the Distinct and Perfect Vehicles.
It is further said:
"Empowered by the spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas, within a single thought-moment one completely encompasses the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This empowerment is distinct from one's own power, and it likewise pertains to the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*).
It further states:
"He attains supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena; his wisdom enters the three periods of time, and his body fills the world, pervading all lands.

Surrounded in the assembly by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-worlds—all of whom are gathered from the various roots of goodness shared by Tathāgatas—they are all said to have fulfilled their great vows and perfected the practices of Bodhisattvas."

In each case, it is stated that they attained as many inconceivable dharma-gates of liberation of all Buddhas as there are atoms in a Buddha-world, or as many as are inconceivable, immeasurable, and so forth, continuing thus through the entirety of the fifth fascicle.

Chapter Two: The Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata. In the second fascicle of this work, when the Tathāgata desires to proclaim the supreme Dharma, he first manifests a supreme sign. Because signs are established in accordance with principle and serve as the manifestation of that principle, he first manifests them as the emblems of principle. Then, all the Bodhisattvas and the lords of all worlds reflect thus:

"What are the ground, the sphere of experience, the power of empowerment, the conduct, the fearlessnesses, the samādhis, and the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind of the Buddhas? What are their lights and sounds, each of which possesses what are called the 'names' of the Buddhas?"
The verse states: "How is it that the Buddha-eye is immeasurable? and so forth.
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, emitted light from between his teeth at his face; from within the light, he spoke these verses, and Bodhisattvas from the ten directions all gathered there.
Within the light of the various bodhisattvas, a verse was spoken, saying: "One employs the benefiting of all sentient beings as the very practice for purifying one's own karma.
It further says: "Within each and every atom, immeasurable bodies appear, manifesting various kinds of adorned buddha-fields."
"All lands throughout the three periods of time can be manifested within a single kṣaṇa.
Furthermore, from within the ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft) of the Tathāgata, a bodhisattva spoke this verse:

"The Buddha-body fills the entire Dharma-realm, Universally appearing before all sentient beings; Responding to conditions and meeting with those who seek him without exception, Yet he ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi."

Within each and every pore of the Tathāgata, Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of all lands sit, surrounded by assemblies of Bodhisattvas, proclaiming the supreme practices of Samantabhadra. This chapter solely elucidates the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Tathāgata, demonstrating how the one embodies the many and how the primary encompasses the dependent.

3. Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Samādhi. To describe the sequence of causes and conditions, he enters the treasury-body (*tathāgata-kośa-garbha*); pointing to the cause to manifest the fruit, it clarifies that the marks have their locus. At that time, Samantabhadra sat upon a lion throne before the Buddha and, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, entered a samādhi called "The Vairocana-Tathāgata Treasury-Body of All Buddhas."

Universally entering the equality of all Buddhas, identical to the ocean of the dharma-realm of empty space, they bring forth all dharmas of samādhi, universally encompassing the dharma-realm of the ten directions.

The ocean of the light of wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time arises from this; it contains and preserves all the powers and liberations of the Buddhas and the wisdom of all Bodhisattvas, and is able to universally accommodate the boundless Dharma-realm within every atom of all lands.
In this way, as it is with Samantabhadra throughout the ten directions and the void of space, so it is with the Dharma-realm.

Within every single atom of all the lands seen by the Buddha-eye, reached by the Buddha’s power, and manifested by the Buddha-body—every one of these atoms contains Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds; within each field are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds; and before each Buddha are Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field, all of whom have entered this samādhi. Before each Samantabhadra, all the Buddhas of the ten directions appear, praising him in unison:
"All Buddhas are identical to you."
The Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously touched his head.
At that time, Samantabhadra arose from samādhi; specifically, he arose from ten gates of samādhi, the fifth being the gate of samādhi of the abodes of all sentient beings.
The verse says:
"The lands he manifests are all adorned and pure; In a single kṣaṇa, he perceives many kalpas.
Samantabhadra dwells peacefully in all lands; The spiritual powers he manifests are unsurpassed."
4. Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World Systems. (This chapter is identical in content to the fourth fascicle.

Since one who possesses the power of transformation must necessarily have those to be transformed, he now demonstrates the objects perceived as the realms for those to be transformed. At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, Samantabhadra universally observed the oceans of all world systems, the oceans of sentient beings, the oceans of all Buddhas, the oceans of the karma of sentient beings, the oceans of faculties and desires, the oceans of the Buddhas’ wheels of Dharma, the oceans of all three periods of time, the oceans of the power of vows, and the oceans of spiritual transformations.
Having observed this, he addressed the bodhisattvas:

"The Buddha’s inconceivable wisdom regarding the purity of the formation and destruction of all world-oceans, and even his inconceivable wisdom regarding the ocean of spiritual transformations that pervades everything—[all these are beyond thought]."
The verse says:
"All buddha-fields enter my body, and the Buddhas who dwell therein are likewise so.
The practices and vows of Samantabhadra are boundless; I have cultivated them and attained their full perfection."
Samantabhadra again addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:

"The Buddhas of the three periods of time have taught that there are ten matters concerning the oceans of worlds. These are: the causes and conditions for the arising of the oceans of worlds; their basis and support; their shape; their essential nature; their adornments; their purification; the eons of the appearance of Buddhas; the eons of their abiding; the distinctions of their transformations; and the gates of their non-distinction. Each of these is as fully detailed as the first phrase."

If explained in detail, they are as numerous as the atoms within oceans of worlds. Furthermore, there are ten causes and conditions by which [these states] have been accomplished, will be accomplished, or are being accomplished:

namely, through the spiritual power of the Buddhas; because the nature of phenomena is thus; through the karma of sentient beings; through the wisdom of Bodhisattvas; through the collective roots of goodness gathered by sentient beings and Bodhisattvas; through the power of the vows of Bodhisattvas to adorn and purify Buddha-fields; through the Bodhisattvas' accomplishment of non-retrogressive conduct and vows; through the Bodhisattvas' mastery over pure resolute conviction; through the outflow of the Tathāgatas' roots of goodness and the sovereign power of all Buddhas at the time of their attainment of enlightenment; and through the sovereign power of Samantabhadra’s vows.
"The detailed explanation is also as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
A verse says:

"Each and every body encompasses all lands; in a single thought-moment, they universally manifest throughout the three periods of time. The Buddha enters into them all through skillful means; this is that which Vairocana has purified and adorned."
It further states:
"There are various bases, forms, essences, and even distinct categories.
[This concludes] Chapter Five: The Flower Treasury World System (Huāzàng Shìjiè Pǐn), Volume 5, pages 89–90.

Although this shows the beings who are the primary objects of transformation, one must know that the lands manifested as their secondary environment are as follows. Samantabhadra addressed the great assembly, saying:

"This Flower Treasury World-Ocean is the world purified by Vairocana Tathāgata when, in the past, during his cultivation of bodhisattva practices throughout world-oceans of kalpas, he approached Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a world-ocean in each and every kalpa; at the site of each Buddha, he purely cultivated world-oceans of great vows to adorn and purify worlds, which are supported by wind-circles as numerous as the atoms in Mount Sumeru."
The verse says:

"Within every single atom of all the worlds in the Flower Treasury, one perceives the entire Dharma-realm; jewel-lights manifest Buddhas gathered like clouds—this is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his buddha-field."
Furthermore, within this ocean of worlds, there is a Great Cakravāḍa mountain range. Within these mountains is ground composed entirely of vajra, adorned with various jewels.

Within the great earth of this ocean of worlds, there are fragrant water seas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, with their bottoms and shores likewise adorned with various jewels.

Each and every fragrant water-ocean contains as many fragrant rivers as there are atoms in the four continents, with banks made of various precious mani-jewels and so forth; within them all appear the causal practices of the Buddhas, and each individual river possesses adornments as numerous as the atoms in a world-system.
This Flower Treasury World-Ocean is adorned with pure merits as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.

Furthermore, within these oceans of fragrant water, which are as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, there abide world-systems as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many fields; each such system contains worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, and their forms and modes of abiding within the ocean of worlds are each different.
The verse says:
"All the vast lands throughout the ten directions entirely enter this world-system.
Although they appear to enter universally from the ten directions, in reality there is neither coming nor entering."
One world-system enters into all, and all enter into one without exception; their essence and characteristics remain as they were, without distinction—inequitable and immeasurable, yet all-pervasive.
"In every atom of all lands, one universally beholds the Tathāgata residing therein.

This ocean of fragrant water is situated within the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha), abiding distributed like the net of Indra; that which is at the very center is named the Ocean of Fragrant Water of Boundless Sublime Flower Light.
In this manner, each of the ten directions is surrounded by twenty layers of worlds as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field.
A verse says:
“The Flower Treasury World-Ocean, equal to the Dharma-realm without distinction, Is supremely pure in its adornments and dwells within space.”

Chapter Six: Vairocana. (Volume Eleven) Having already provided a general demonstration of both the supporting environment and the supported inhabitants, as well as the primary and secondary aspects, it is now necessary to specifically distinguish the partial traces of a single direction. By citing the partial to know the perfect, and by showing the particular to recognize the universal, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the great assembly, saying:
"In the remote past, beyond world-microdust kalpas, and even twice that number, there was an ocean of worlds named Universal Gate Radiance."
Within this ocean of worlds, there is a world named Victorious Sound, which rests upon an ocean of mani flowers and has as many worlds as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru as its retinue.

Its shape is perfectly circular, and its ground is adorned with immeasurable splendors; it is surrounded by three hundred tiers of jewels, and jeweled clouds cover it above like Mount Sumeru. Clothing and food arrive according to one's thoughts.

In that world of Supreme Sound, there is a sea of fragrant water named Pure Radiance. Within it appears a great lotus Sumeru mountain named Flower Flame Universal Adornment Banner Mountain, upon which is a forest named Maṇi Flower, adorned with various jewels.
It was surrounded on all sides by hundreds of billions of nayutas of cities, where various sentient beings dwelt.
To the east of the forest was a city named Jvālāprabha, the capital of a human king, which was likewise surrounded on all sides by hundreds of billions of nayutas of cities.

In the first eon of that world of Exquisite Sound, there appeared as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten Mount Sumerus. The name of the first Buddha was Supreme Cloud of Mount Sumeru of All Merits; his king’s name was Joyful Vision of Good Wisdom, who ruled over a hundred trillion nayutas of cities. He had thirty-seven thousand ladies and courtiers, five hundred princes headed by Great Majestic Radiance, and ten thousand wives.

When the Prince saw the light, by the power of the roots of goodness he had previously cultivated, he realized ten Dharma-gates and spoke these verses; through the Buddha’s spiritual power, their sound pervaded the entire world of Supreme Sound.

Having heard this, the king, together with his consort, came to where the Buddha was; the eight classes of followers all assembled there, and upon hearing the Dharma, they obtained benefit: Mahātejas attained the light of immeasurable wisdom.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there appeared the Buddha Puṇyapāramitakuśalamūlavyūha; at that time, the youth Mahātejaḥprabha beheld the Buddha and immediately attained ten thousand dharma-gates, including the mindfulness-of-the-Buddha samādhi known as the "Gate of the Boundless Ocean-Treasury."

"Encountering the third and fourth Buddhas, he obtained benefit and returned to his original abode. The above, from the "Samādhi of Samantabhadra" onwards, was all spoken by the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

2. The Sixth Section Spoken in the Hall of Universal Radiance, Volume Four, Second Assembly: The Sixth Section Spoken in the Hall of Universal Radiance, Volume Four, Part 7. Chapter 7: The Names and Titles of the Tathāgatas (Rulai Minghao Pin), Volume Twelve.

Although one knows the distinct principle of partial manifestation in a single direction, it is only within the distinct Bodhimandas of the ten directions that one attains perfect enlightenment; thus, sitting upon the Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne in the Hall of Universal Radiance, one’s wondrous realization becomes fully perfected.

He was accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, all of whom were in their final birth before attaining enlightenment (*ekajātipratibaddha*), having gathered here from other directions.

For the sake of causing sentient beings to forever sever all afflictions (*kleśa*), he taught the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten treasuries (*kośa*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten vows (*praṇidhāna*), the ten concentrations (*samādhi*), the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the ten summits (*mūrdhan*). Furthermore, he taught the realm of the Tathāgata’s ground, the range of his spiritual powers, his powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), samādhis, supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), the unimpeded mastery of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, eloquence (*pratibhāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and supreme vows—all of which are termed "Tathāgata."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, manifested supernatural powers; then, in each of the ten directions, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, there was a Buddha from a world accompanied by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, who all came to where the Buddha was.
In the eastern world-realm named Golden, there is a leading bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī. Empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, he surveyed the bodhisattvas and spoke these words:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

The Buddha-fields, the abiding of the Buddhas, the adornment of the Buddha-lands, the nature of the Buddha-dharma, the purity of the Buddha-lands, the preaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas, the appearance of the Buddhas, the accomplishment of the Buddha-lands, and the awakening of the Buddhas are all inconceivable.
Why is this? The Buddha, throughout the ten directions, knows all sentient beings and preaches the Dharma to subdue them according to what is appropriate for each.

Regarding this Sahā world, the Tathāgata observes the various bodies, names, and physical forms; the diverse lifespans, whether long or short; the locations, the faculties, the places of birth, and the various karmas of all beings within the four continents of the four quarters, and describes them all as "various," so that what each sentient being perceives is different.
Within these four continents, the Tathāgata may be known by ten thousand names, such as Sarvārthasiddha, Paripūrṇacandra, Śākyamuni, Vairocana, and so forth.
In this manner, each of the four continents throughout the ten directions has ten thousand names for its respective world-system;
yet within these ten billion sets of four continents in this Sahā world-system, there are hundreds of billions of millions of various names.

Furthermore, outside of this Sahā world, there is in each of the ten directions a world, each having hundreds of billions of millions of various names; throughout the entirety of the space of the ten directions, they are all diverse and distinct.
Chapter Eight: The Four Noble Truths.
Having already distinguished the person, one should know the distinct dharmas. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the various bodhisattvas:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
The Noble Truth of Suffering is, in this Sahā world, sometimes called sin, sometimes called oppression, and sometimes called transformation, clinging, accumulation, or thorn.
The noble truth of origination is alternatively termed "bondage," "destruction," "the sense of craving and attachment," "erroneous conceptualization," and so forth.
The noble truth of cessation is alternatively termed "non-contention," "freedom from dust," "quiescence," and so forth.
The Noble Truth of the Path is also called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the Tendency toward Quiescence (*śamathābhimukha*), the Guide, and so forth.
In this manner, each of the worlds throughout the ten directions has four hundred billion ten thousand such names.
Chapter Nine: The Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance. Volume Thirteen. Desiring to proclaim the Dharma, he first moved their hearts;

[the light] extended horizontally to fill empty space and vertically reached the pinnacle of the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*). To clarify the person and the Dharma, and to define the scope of its reach, at that time the World-Honored One emitted light from beneath his feet, illuminating ten billion four-continent worlds (*cāturdvīpa*) and even ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens. By the Buddha’s spiritual power, all beheld the Tathāgata surrounded by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields. From each of the ten directions came one Great Bodhisattva, each accompanied by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, with Mañjuśrī at their head.
At that time, Mañjuśrī in every location simultaneously spoke verses before each Buddha.

At that moment, the light passed beyond this world to as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields; in each of these, from the four continents up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, Mañjuśrī likewise spoke verses in every place. This was also the case throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattvas’ Questions on Clarifying Wisdom. This chapter consists of ten fascicles.
Desiring to shatter ignorance, one must first address its initial sprout.

Since both the questioner and the respondent are Great Beings (*mahāsattva*), it is said that this marks the beginning of the ranks of the Bodhisattva assembly; therefore, the opening is designated with the phrase: "At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Buddhamati."
“O Son of the Buddha!
The nature of the mind is one; how can there be such various distinctions?
Namely: the good and evil realms of rebirth, the completeness or deficiency of the sense faculties, the similarities and differences in taking birth, and beauty or ugliness, suffering or happiness.”

The mind does not know karma, and karma does not know the mind; sensation does not know retribution, and retribution does not know sensation; the mind does not know sensation, and sensation does not know the mind; the cause does not know the condition, and the condition does not know the cause; wisdom does not know the object, and the object does not know wisdom.
Bodhirāja replied:
"All phenomena are devoid of activity and lack any intrinsic nature; therefore, they are all mutually unaware of one another."
Just as the waters in a river rush forward in a turbulent current, each unaware of the others, so too are all phenomena (*dharmas*).
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and the various faculties of perception—by means of these they constantly circulate, yet there is nothing that can move them.
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally without arising; it manifests as having arising, yet herein there is neither a subject that manifests nor an object that is manifested.
Whether real or unreal, whether false or non-false, whether mundane or supramundane, there exists only conventional verbal expression.
Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Vasumitra:
"O Son of the Buddha!

Since all sentient beings are not [truly] sentient beings, how does the Tathāgata, according to their time, life-span, body, conduct, understanding, speech, and mental inclinations, through skillful means and contemplative observation, manifest his body within each of these classes of sentient beings to teach and discipline them?"
Dhanapati replied in verse:
"Discerningly observe the internal body: who herein is 'I'?
If one can understand in this way, they will realize the existence and non-existence of the self."
Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī:

"All sentient beings equally possess the four great elements; they are without self and without what belongs to a self. How is it that there is the experience of suffering and pleasure, beauty and ugliness, internal and external conditions, and retribution in the present life and in future lives?"
"However, within the Dharma-realm there is neither beauty nor evil.
Ratnaśrī spoke in verse:
"Just as a pure, bright mirror, according to the object it faces, manifests images that each differ, so too is the nature of karma."
Just as within the womb all the sense faculties are fully formed, yet their physical forms have no place from which they come, so too is the nature of karma.
Just as within the hells there are various kinds of suffering, yet none of them have any source from which they arise, so too is the nature of karma.
Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa:

"The Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is but a single Dharma; why then do you speak of immeasurable dharmas, manifest immeasurable lands, transform immeasurable assemblies, proclaim immeasurable sounds, display immeasurable bodies, know immeasurable minds, manifest immeasurable supernormal powers, and shake immeasurable worlds—all of which you describe as 'immeasurable'?"
Guṇaketu replied in verse:
"Just as the nature of fire is one, yet it can burn all things, and the flames are without discrimination—such is the Dharma of all Buddhas."
The ocean waves, the wind-blown [clouds], and the rain-soaked earth are also like this.
Furthermore, just as the single element of earth can produce various kinds of sprouts, yet there is no distinction within the earth itself, so too are the qualities of all Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Mūrdhagata:
"The Tathāgata’s field of merit is equal and without distinction; why, then, do you perceive that the fruits of the giving of sentient beings are different?"

Regarding what are called various forms and shapes, families and lineages, wealth and masters, retinues, official ranks, merits, and wisdom—all these are termed "various"; yet the Tathāgata’s mind toward them is equanimous, free from any discriminatory thought.
Mukhāgrya replied with a verse:
"Just as the single great earth produces sprouts according to each seed, yet harbors neither enmity nor favoritism toward them, so too is the Buddha’s field of merit."
It is also like water of a single taste that appears different according to the vessel; it is also like a pure, bright mirror that manifests images in accordance with the objects before it.
It is like the *agada* medicine, which can cure all diseases—the latter two lines are largely the same.
Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Vīradatta:
"The Buddha's teaching is one; yet, when sentient beings perceive it, why do they not immediately sever all afflictions?"
However, since the five aggregates, the three realms, and the three poisons are without distinction, the Buddha's teaching may be beneficial for some sentient beings and not beneficial for others.
He replied:
"It is due to the differences between diligence and indolence that these various [states] are produced.
Then Mañjuśrī questioned the Bodhisattva Dharmottara:
“As the Buddha has taught, if there are sentient beings who uphold the True Dharma, they are all able to sever and eliminate all afflictions.
For what reason, then, are there those who uphold the True Dharma yet do not sever them, but instead follow along with the various afflictions?”
Dharmottara replied:
"It is like a person drifting on water who, fearing drowning, dies of thirst;
so it is with one who possesses much learning but does not practice the Dharma."
It is like a person who prepares a delicious meal but starves himself and does not eat;
like a person skilled in medicinal prescriptions who cannot cure his own illness;
or like a person who counts another's treasures while possessing not even half a coin for himself.
It is like one born into a royal palace who suffers from hunger and cold;
it is like a deaf person playing music to delight others while not hearing it oneself;
it is like a blind person painting various images to show them to others while not seeing them oneself—the latter two lines are identical in meaning.
Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī:

"In the Buddha-dharma, wisdom is foremost; for what reason does the Tathāgata sometimes praise giving, morality, and even wisdom as well as the four immeasurable minds, yet never state that enlightenment can be accomplished by means of a single dharma alone?"
Jñānaśīri replied in verse:

“The Buddha knows the minds of sentient beings, whose natures and dispositions are each different; according to what is appropriate for their deliverance, he teaches the Dharma as if treating them accordingly.”
"To those who are stingy, he praises such dharmas as generosity.
Mañjuśrī asked Samantabhadra Bodhisattva:
"If all Buddhas attain liberation through only a single path, why do we now see that their Buddha-fields are not the same?"
The Wise One (Bhadramukha) replied in verse:
"Mañjuśrī, the Dharma is always thus: the Dharma King has but this one Dharma; all those who are unimpeded give birth from and transcend birth-and-death through this single path."
The bodies of all Buddhas are but a single Dharma-body; their single mind and single wisdom, as well as their powers and fearlessnesses, are likewise one.
The lands of all Buddhas are fully adorned and perfected; yet according to the different actions of sentient beings, they appear in various ways.
"The Buddha-fields are without discrimination; there is neither aversion nor affection. It is only according to the minds of sentient beings that they see such differences.
Then, for the tenth time, he addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"We have finished speaking; you, O Benevolent One, should now speak of the realm of the Tathāgata."
"What is this Buddha-realm, its causal deliverance, its entry into wisdom, its teaching of the Dharma, its realization through knowledge, and its manifestation of the vast—all as in the first phrase?
Mañjuśrī also answered with ten verses:
"The profound realm of the Tathāgata is equal in measure to empty space."
All sentient beings enter it, yet in reality there is nothing entered.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s profound realm and all its supreme and wondrous causes, even if one were to proclaim them for billions of eons, one could not exhaust them. The remaining nine [categories] are all answered by means of ultimate non-differentiation.

Because of this answer, throughout the entire realm of empty space in the ten directions of the Sahā world, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, all clearly perceived ten kinds of distinctions. These are: the distinction of dharmas, karma, the world, the body-faculties, birth, the fruit of upholding the precepts, the fruit of violating the precepts, and the fruit of the land—the latter nine phrases being identical to the first.
11. Chapter on Pure Conduct (Śīla-varga). Volume fourteen of eleven [in this section].
Although one may understand the destination, one cannot advance without practice.
Because it involves departing from the mundane and progressing toward the Path, it is called "pure"; it purifies those very practices.
By practicing this provisional purity, both parties attain the designation of "pure conduct. Jñānaśrī asked Mañjuśrī:
"O Son of the Buddha!

How does one obtain the state where the actions of body, speech, and mind are free from fault; where they are non-harming, indestructible, unbreakable, non-retrogressive, immovable, supremely pure, and preceded by untainted wisdom—possessing these qualities as described in the first phrase?"
How does one obtain fulfillment in the place of birth, lineage, family, physical appearance, mindfulness, wisdom, conduct, fearlessness, and awakening—how are all these fulfilled?

Because the worlds are not the same, he thus distinguishes their various practices. At that time, the Tathāgata was in the Universal Radiance Hall at the site of enlightenment, seated upon the lion throne; his wondrous awakening was fully perfected, and he had first attained his distinct names, such as "He Who Has Forever Severed the Two Practices," and so forth.

Together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddha-fields—all of whom were in their final birth—they came from other directions to praise the virtues of the Buddha.
At that time, Samantabhadra entered the Buddha-Flower Adornment Samādhi. Emerging from this samādhi, the Bodhisattva Samantamati asked: "What constitutes the reliance of a bodhisattva?
What constitutes the extraordinary conception?"
What is the practice of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who exerts diligent effort and attains peace of mind?
What is their ethical discipline (śīla)?
What is their accomplishment of sentient beings, their entry into realms (dhātu), their entry into eons (kalpa), and so forth—these two hundred questions.
Samantabhadra’s extensive responses all contain profound meanings.
In the response concerning the "extraordinary perception," it says:
"One should conceive of all practices as one's own practice; one's vows should likewise be so."
The answer is that there are ten kinds of peace of mind, all of which arise from one’s own practice enabling others to attain it, whereby the mind becomes peaceful.

Regarding the precepts, there are ten kinds of precepts that are entirely for the benefit of others: namely, the precept of not abandoning the bodhicitta, the precept of distancing oneself from the stages of the two vehicles, the precept of observing the benefit of sentient beings, and so forth.

There are ten kinds of self-knowledge of receiving the prediction [of enlightenment], namely: generating the bodhicitta through superior resolve; never becoming weary of or abandoning the practices of all bodhisattvas; dwelling through all kalpas performing the bodhisattva practices; cultivating all Buddha-dharmas; having single-minded, profound faith in all the Buddha-teachings; cultivating all roots of goodness so that they are fully accomplished; establishing all sentient beings in the Bodhi of the Buddhas; being in harmonious non-duality with spiritual friends; regarding spiritual friends as Tathāgatas; and constantly and diligently guarding the words of one’s original vow for Bodhi—each of these includes the self-knowledge of receiving the prediction.

There are ten kinds of entries into the bodhisattvas, ten kinds of entries into the Tathāgatas, ten kinds of entries into the conduct of sentient beings, ten kinds of entries into worlds, ten kinds of entries into eons, and even ten kinds of Buddhas—namely, the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha of Vows, the Buddha of Karmic Retribution, the Buddha of Sustenance, the Buddha of Nirvāṇa, the Buddha of the Dharma-realm, the Buddha of Mind, the Buddha of Samādhi, the Buddha of Original Nature, and the Buddha of Following Delight.
The ten causes and conditions for generating the bodhicitta all take sentient beings as primary.
In scroll fifty-four, there are ten kinds of groves: birth and death are the grove of the bodhisattva, because they never grow weary of or abandon them.

Without wearying in the transformation of sentient beings, he dwells throughout kalpas to gather and practice; he abides in the purification of buddha-lands and subdues others within the palaces of Māra; he contemplates the Dharma and observes its principles, continuing the succession of all Buddha-dharmas through his practices; he performs the act of turning the wheel of Dharma and accomplishes the Way in a single thought-moment.

In the fifty-fifth fascicle, there are ten kinds of generating the immeasurable, boundless, and vast mind. Regarding all Buddha-fields, observing the realms of all sentient beings, observing all lands, all worlds, and all dharma-realms, observing that all dharmas are like space, the vast practices of all Bodhisattvas, maintaining right mindfulness of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, observing the inconceivable fruits of various karmic retributions, adorning and purifying all Buddha-lands, universally entering all great assemblies of Buddhas, and observing the wondrous voices of all Tathāgatas—all these are called "generating the vast mind."

○ Scroll 56: Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of unimpeded functions (*anāvaraṇa-prayoga*), namely: the unimpeded function regarding sentient beings; the unimpeded function regarding lands, the dharma-body, vows, objective spheres, wisdom, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*); and the power [of these], as in the first phrase.

Regarding the unimpeded function of the body, there are ten aspects: the unimpeded function of causing the bodies of all sentient beings to enter one’s own body; one’s own body entering the bodies of all sentient beings; the bodies of all Buddhas entering the body of a single Buddha; the body of a single Buddha entering the bodies of all Buddhas; all lands entering one’s own body; manifesting the bodies of sentient beings of the three periods of time with a single body; manifesting boundless bodies with a single body; entering samādhi and manifesting from a single body as many bodies as there are sentient beings; attaining perfect enlightenment and manifesting the bodies of all sentient beings within the body of a single sentient being; manifesting the body of a single sentient being within the bodies of all sentient beings; and all sentient beings manifesting the Dharma-body, and the Dharma-body manifesting the bodies of all sentient beings, just as in the first case.

Volume 57: Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): the habitual tendency of the bodhicitta; of roots of goodness; of miraculous birth; of beholding Buddhas; of taking birth; of vows and practices; of the various perfections (*pāramitā*); of contemplation; of the equal Dharma; and of the distinctions of spheres of experience.

There are ten kinds of eyes: the fleshly eye, because it sees all forms; the celestial eye, because it sees the minds of sentient beings; the wisdom eye, because it sees the faculties of sentient beings; the Dharma eye, because it sees the true mark; the Buddha eye, because it sees the ten powers of a Buddha; the knowledge eye, because it sees all phenomena; the light-emitting eye, because it sees the radiance of the Buddha; the eye that transcends birth and death, because it sees nirvana; the unimpeded eye, because there is no obstruction in what it sees; and the eye of omniscience, because it sees the universal gate of the dharma-realm.

There are ten kinds of ears: hearing voices of praise, one does not become attached; hearing voices of disparagement, one does not give rise to anger; hearing discourses on the Two Vehicles, one does not seek them nor become attached to them; hearing of the Bodhisattva path, one rejoices with exuberant joy; hearing of the sufferings of hell, one gives rise to great compassion; hearing discourses on humans and devas, one knows their impermanence; hearing praise of the Buddhas’ fulfillment of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*), one hears it; hearing discourses on the six perfections and the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one resolves to practice them; hearing the sounds of the ten directions, one penetrates their profound and subtle meanings; and from the first thought-moment to the final thought-moment, one constantly hears the True Dharma and never abandons sentient beings.

There are ten kinds of noses: hearing foul odors without aversion; hearing fragrant scents without attachment; maintaining an equanimous mind toward both fragrance and foulness; abiding in impartiality when hearing neither fragrance nor foulness; hearing the environments and inhabitants of sentient beings and knowing their karmic actions; hearing of all hidden treasures and being able to discern them; hearing of births in the six realms and knowing their transgressions and practices; hearing of the conduct of Śrāvakas and abiding in omniscience; hearing of the conduct of Bodhisattvas and employing an impartial mind; and hearing of the wisdom of all Buddhas without abandoning the Bodhisattva practice.

There are ten kinds of tongues: the tongue that reveals the conduct of all sentient beings; the tongue that reveals inexhaustible Dharma-gates; the tongue that praises the virtues of all Buddhas; the tongue that expounds unimpeded eloquence; the tongue that elucidates the aids to the Path of the Mahāyāna; the tongue that universally covers the void of the ten directions; the tongue that universally illumines all lands; the tongue that causes all sentient beings to attain awakening and understanding; the tongue that causes all Buddhas to rejoice; and the tongue that subdues demons and outsiders, leading them to Nirvāṇa.

There are ten kinds of bodies: the human body manifests as a human; the non-human body manifests as the three evil realms; the celestial body manifests throughout the three realms; the body of one in training (*śaikṣa*) appears on the stage of training; the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) manifests the stage of an arhat; the pratyekabuddha body manifests the stage of a pratyekabuddha; the bodhisattva body accomplishes the Mahāyāna; the tathāgata body is consecrated by the water of wisdom; the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) is skillfully produced; and the untainted dharma-body (*anāsrava-dharmakāya*) manifests the bodies of all sentient beings through the path of effortlessness.

There are ten kinds of mentalities: the leading mentality, which initiates roots of goodness; the settled mentality, which is deeply faithful and unshakable; the penetrating mentality, which accords with and understands the Buddha-dharma; the internally aware mentality, which knows the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings; the undisturbed mentality, which is not mixed with various delusions; the luminous and pure mentality, which is untainted by adventitious defilements; the mentality that observes sentient beings, never missing a single moment; the mentality of skillful discernment in action, never giving rise to a fault in any situation; the mentality of closely guarding the sense faculties, being tamed and without distraction; and the mentality of skillfully entering samādhi, entering the samādhi of the Buddhas.
There are ten [qualities] for each of the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
There are ten kinds of lion’s roars, namely: proclaiming, "I shall certainly attain Buddhahood," which is the great lion’s roar of the bodhicitta.
"The four [vows] beginning with 'I shall cause all sentient beings who have not yet crossed over to cross over' are the Great Compassionate One’s Great Lion’s Roar.
'I shall cause the Three Jewels to never be severed' is the Great Lion’s Roar that repays the Buddha’s kindness."
“I shall adorn and purify all lands” is the ultimate, firm vow, the great lion’s roar.
“I shall eliminate all evil realms and places of hardship” is the great lion’s roar of personally upholding pure precepts.
"I shall fulfill the three karmas of all Buddhas and their marks of adornment"—this is the great lion’s roar of insatiable merit.
"I shall eliminate all celestial Māras and all demonic activities"—this is the great lion’s roar of practicing correct conduct to sever all afflictions.
"I shall eliminate 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' and purify the three gates of emptiness"—this is the great lion’s roar of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
That a Bodhisattva in his final birth manifests birth in a royal palace, renounces the world, and attains enlightenment—this is the great lion’s roar of practicing according to the teaching.
In fifty-eight fascicles, there are ten sections each for the six perfections; their dharma-characteristics are generally broad and expansive, yet they mostly belong to specific categories.
The same applies to the ten sections each for the four immeasurables.

There are ten ways of seeking the Dharma: with a straightforward mind and diligence, one exclusively severs the delusions of others, benefits oneself and others, enters into wisdom, emerges from birth and death, acts for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, severs the doubts of others, and fulfills the Buddha-dharma.

The ten māras, the ten deeds of Māra, the ten deeds that abandon Māra, and the ten kinds of things sustained by Māra: namely, being sustained by the māra of indolence; having narrow and inferior aspirations; being satisfied with meager practice; accepting only one [vehicle] and not others; failing to make great vows; delighting in solitary cessation and the severance of delusions; seeking the eternal cessation of birth and death; abandoning the conduct of a bodhisattva; failing to transform sentient beings; and doubting and slandering the True Dharma.

There are ten kinds of being sustained by the Buddhas: namely, being sustained by the Buddhas upon first generating the bodhicitta; not losing the bodhicitta; being able to recognize and depart from demonic activities; hearing the Dharma and practicing according to what was taught; knowing suffering without becoming weary of it; contemplating profound dharmas to attain the fruit; preaching the Lesser Vehicle without taking realization as the final goal; contemplating the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) without dwelling therein; reaching the state of non-arising while intentionally taking birth; and giving rise to practice through the realization of wisdom.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven, there are ten kinds of activities to be performed.
When about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born, they manifest ten kinds of events.

In the fifty-ninth fascicle, it is stated that there are ten matters regarding the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of dwelling in the womb; this is for the sake of perfecting those sentient beings of small minds and inferior understanding, so as not to allow them to give rise to the thought that the Bodhisattva is spontaneously transformed by supernatural birth.
In order to bring to maturity his parents, kinsmen, and those with whom he shared roots of goodness in past lives, he manifested a smile and took seven steps.

He manifested dwelling in the stage of childhood, dwelling in the royal palace, leaving home and practicing austerities, proceeding to the tree of enlightenment, sitting at the site of awakening, subduing Māra and attaining Buddhahood, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa; each of these stages comprised ten specific events.

Chapter 9: The First Chapter on the Exposition at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, Volume 21; Ninth Assembly: The First Chapter on the Exposition at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, Volume 21. Section 39: The Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm, Volume 60.
Although knowledge is manifold, it does not transcend the *dharmadhātu*.
The *dharmadhātu* is non-dual, yet it manifests differentiations spontaneously.

Differentiated knowledge constitutes the function of the *dharmadhātu*, while non-differentiated knowledge constitutes its essence. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the Greatly Adorned Multi-storied Hall at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī, together with five hundred bodhisattvas, with Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī as their leaders.

Having listed one hundred and forty bodhisattvas and others, all of whom had fully accomplished the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, and having extensively praised their virtues, at that time the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those bodhisattvas, manifested a body of great compassion through the power of skillful means to fill the void of space; having entered the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi, the entire world was universally purified and adorned.
The Great Adorned Pavilion suddenly became vast and expansive, without boundaries and adorned with various jewels.

Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, the Jeta Grove suddenly became vast and expansive, equal in measure to as many Buddha-lands as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, and was likewise adorned with various jewels.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses inconceivable and sovereign powers.

Beyond world-oceans as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there is a single world, a single Buddha, and a single Bodhisattva; together with a multitude of Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in those world-oceans, they have all come, each manifesting their own spiritual transformations.

By the power of the Buddha, in a single moment of thought at the site of one Buddha, they universally beheld the ten directions without any confusion; in a mere instant, they were able to travel to them all. Thus, bodhisattvas such as these filled the Jeta Grove.

At that time, Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas were in the Jeta Grove, yet none of them perceived the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, the Tathāgata’s realm of majestic excellence, his playful transformations, his sublime conduct, or his majestic abiding in the purification of buddha-fields. Furthermore, they did not perceive the inconceivable realm of the bodhisattvas, nor did they see the great assembly of bodhisattvas; all these things remained unseen because their roots of goodness were dissimilar. Specifically, they had originally failed to cultivate the roots of goodness for beholding the Buddha, had originally failed to praise and proclaim the merits of the buddha-fields and the supernatural transformations of the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and had originally lacked the various practices such as generating the bodhicitta within saṃsāra, causing others to abide in the bodhicitta, and ensuring that the lineage of the Tathāgatas would not be severed. Since all such qualities were fundamentally absent in them, they saw nothing.
For this reason, they are unable to see, hear, or even think [of it], because they have attained liberation by relying on the Śrāvaka vehicle.

It is like the immeasurable hungry ghosts on the banks of the Ganges who, tormented by thirst, seek water but cannot find it; though they dwell by the river's edge, they do not see the river, and even if some should see it, they see only it as parched dry.
The Śrāvakas are likewise.

For example, suppose a person in a great assembly dreams of seeing the summit of Mount Sumeru, adorned in various ways, where devas enjoy pleasures; they also see themselves in that same place as one of those people in the assembly of devas. Yet, those [other people] do not see them, because they did not dream it.
The śrāvakas are likewise.
For example, although the Snowy Mountains are endowed with various medicinal herbs, only a skilled physician perceives them, whereas hunters and herdsmen do not.
Similarly, when a bhikṣu enters a meditative absorption on the universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) amidst a great assembly, the rest of the assembly does not perceive it at all.

Just as when a person is born, there are two deities who constantly follow them: one is called "Born Together" (sahaja) and the second is called "Same Name" (samānanāman). These deities always see the person, but the person does not see the deities.

At that time, ten bodhisattvas, including the Bodhisattva Vairocana-praṇidhāna-raśmi, each spoke ten verses to exhort the śrāvakas to contemplate the Tathāgata and all the bodhisattvas, describing the inconceivable phenomena and principles of the Tathāgatas and bodhisattvas.
In the very first chapter of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, there is a single verse that rebukes the śrāvakas, saying:
"All the pratyekabuddhas and those great śrāvakas are entirely unable to know the sphere of the bodhisattva's practice."
The intent of these verses largely elucidates the functions of the perfect cause and the perfect fruit.

At that time, in the sixty-first fascicle, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva surveyed the entire assembly and, by means of skillful means equal to the dharma-realm, skillful means equal to the realm of empty space, skillful means equal to the realm of sentient beings, and skillful means equal to the light and shadows of all phenomena, spoke for the sake of the bodhisattvas upon ten dharma-phrases concerning this Lion-Stretching Samādhi, extensively clarifying the supreme functions of mastery over the primary and secondary realms.

At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to cause all bodhisattvas to dwell securely in this samādhi, emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows a great radiance called "The Door of Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm of the Three Times," which shone everywhere upon all buddha-lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Having fully elucidated the spiritual power of the Tathāgata, it then says:
"Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, wishes to proclaim once more these various miraculous transformations that occurred within the Jeta Grove."
And he spoke in verse:

"You should behold this Jetavana Grove; through the boundless majestic power of the Buddha, all manner of adornments are manifested, filling the dharma-realm of the ten directions," and so forth, in twenty-six lines of verse, praising what had been seen previously.

At that time, because they were illuminated by the light of the Buddha’s samādhi, the bodhisattvas immediately entered such a samādhi and attained the unspeakable gate of great compassion; they performed buddha-work throughout the ten directions to subdue and transform sentient beings.
At that time, Mañjuśrī emerged from the Hall of Good Abiding; having made various offerings to the Buddha, he took his leave and traveled south toward the human realm.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, saw Mañjuśrī and the bodhisattvas departing from the Jeta Grove to wander among the people, and he thought to himself:
"I shall now go with them to the southern region."
Then Śāriputra, together with six thousand bhikṣus, departed from their dwelling and went to where the Buddha was. He reported everything in detail to the World-Honored One.
Having received the World-Honored One’s permission, he circumambulated him to the right and departed, proceeding to where Mañjuśrī was.

These six thousand bhikṣus were those with whom Śāriputra himself had lived; they had not long since left the household life—namely, the bhikṣus Sāgarabuddhi, Sujāta, Puṇyaprabha, Vidyudbhava, Caritracandra, and Devaśrī—and none of them were categorized among those of the Hīnayāna.

These six thousand individuals have all made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, deeply planted roots of goodness, possessed vast power of understanding, and had clear vision of faith. Their minds were expansive and broad; they contemplated the realm of the Buddhas, realized the fundamental nature of phenomena, and benefited sentient beings. They always delighted in diligently seeking the merits of all Buddhas—all this was due to the teaching and transformation through the Dharma by Mañjuśrī.
Śāriputra caused the bhikṣus to contemplate Mañjuśrī’s pure physical marks and the perfection of his assembly.

Upon hearing this, the minds of the bhikṣus became pure and their faith and understanding grew firm; their entire bodies leaped with joy, all their afflictions and sufferings were eliminated, they were endowed with the faculties of a bodhisattva, attained the power of a bodhisattva, and entered the profound realm.
He said, "Great Master,
you are leading us to the presence of the Victorious One.
When Śāriputra had arrived at Mañjuśrī’s location, he said:
"These bhikṣus wish to have an audience with you.
The bhikṣus said to Mañjuśrī,
"May we all obtain that which you, O Benevolent One, have obtained."
Mañjuśrī exhorted him with ten matters, causing him to practice the path of bodhi. Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus immediately attained the Samādhi of Unobstructed Vision;

they beheld the realms of all Buddhas, seeing in their entirety the various environments and bodies of all Buddhas. They knew the ten prior and subsequent births of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, remembered ten kalpas of past and future within those realms, and recalled the ten previous lives of those Tathāgatas—each consisting of ten aspects: attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, performing miraculous transformations, and preaching the Dharma. Furthermore, they immediately accomplished ten thousand samādhis.
Mañjuśrī then exhorted the bhikṣus to abide in the conduct of Samantabhadra; thus it is known that what they had attained did not yet enter the conduct of Samantabhadra.

When five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, five hundred boys, and five hundred girls had all assembled in the city of Puṇyavatī, among those five hundred boys, Sudhana was the leader.

Mañjuśrī then observed the causes and conditions for Sudhana’s name and so forth; having understood these causes and conditions, he further knew that the youth had already made offerings to Buddhas in the past, had deeply planted roots of goodness, and was a fit vessel for the Buddha-dharma.

Sudhana asked:

Mañjuśrī further exhorted him to draw near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra).
"From here, traveling south, there is the country of Uttarakuru; on Mount Sudarśana, there dwells the bhikṣu Meghaśrī," and so forth.

my eye of faith is pure, and the light of wisdom shines radiantly. I travel to the lands of the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas and uphold all Buddha-dharmas."
"Good son!

I have only attained this Dharma-door of the Universal Vision of the Radiance of Wisdom that Recollects the Realms of All Buddhas; how could I possibly fathom the boundless gates of pure conduct and wisdom of the great Bodhisattvas?"
He extensively elucidated the dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, whereby one perceives all lands and all Buddhas within a single thought-moment.
He then dispatched the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha to travel south to the country of Samudramukha.
Sudhana, single-mindedly mindful of the instructions of the spiritual friend and the dharma-gate, arrived at the abode of Samudrareṇu and saw him, and so forth.
He asked:
"How does one abandon the stage of an ordinary person and enter the stage of a Tathāgata? and so on.
Sāgaramegha said:
"I have resided here for twelve years, constantly taking the great ocean as my sphere of activity.
I contemplate the great ocean as vast, immeasurable, profoundly deep, and difficult to fathom, gradually becoming deeper and broader."
When I was contemplating in this way, a lotus flower appeared in the great ocean, and within the flower, a Buddha appeared and taught me the Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye.
I know only this Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye.
The bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita dwelt in the coastal village of Laṅkāmārga. When Sudhana arrived there, he saw this bhikṣu coming and going through the air. The bhikṣu said to Sudhana:

"I have accomplished the liberation door of non-obstruction; I perceive the mental activities and conduct of all sentient beings without any hindrance, and I have attained mastery in making offerings to all Buddhas."

Sudhana asked, "What are their characteristics?

The eighty-first, Sudhana, having received the instructions of Maitreya, traveled gradually through one hundred and ten cities until he reached the city of Sumana in the country of Samantamukha. Standing at its gate, he contemplated Mañjuśrī while observing him with compliant attention.

At that time, Mañjuśrī extended his right hand from afar across one hundred and ten yojanas, placed it upon Sudhana’s head, preached the Dharma for him, and caused him to enter the practice site of Samantabhadra’s conduct.
Mañjuśrī withdrew and became invisible.

Thereupon, Sudhana reflected and contemplated, single-mindedly aspiring to see Mañjuśrī and to behold and serve as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in the great trichiliocosm. Longing to see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, he then, before the lion throne in the Vajragarbha Bodhimaṇḍa upon a seat of universal jewel-lotus treasury, gave rise to a vast mind equal to the realm of empty space. Having seen ten kinds of auspicious signs and ten kinds of radiant manifestations, he gathered all his faculties and sought with one-pointed mind to behold [Samantabhadra].

At that time, Sudhana saw Samantabhadra seated upon a lion throne before the Tathāgata, most preeminent among the assembly of all bodhisattvas; from each and every pore issued forth rays of light as numerous as motes of dust, pervading all worlds throughout space, extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings and giving rise to great joy.
Furthermore, in every moment of thought, various clouds of fragrance emerge, pervading the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, extensively performing the Buddha-work.
Having seen this, one immediately becomes endowed with the ten pāramitās.

Samantabhadra touched his head with his hand, and he immediately attained samādhi-doors as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-lands; he saw Samantabhadra in this very same manner within every single atom throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
